entries.condition: Sentence-level LRS2, not LRW; dilation mentioned only in related work on translation and synthesis.
entries.quote: (FC-10), and a deeper one with 15 convolutional layers

questions.q: What benchmark gains does the paper actually report, and against which prior results?
questions.answer: The authors claim absolute gains of 1.2 points on LRW and 3.2 on LRW-1000. Table 1 lists 85.3% on LRW and 41.4% on LRW-1000; the strongest prior LRW entry shown is 84.1%, while the cited LRW-1000 prior entries are 38.23% and 36.9%. The paper also claims a 1.9% gain over baseline [15].

questions.q: Does variable-length training improve accuracy, robustness, or both?
questions.answer: For BGRU, variable-length training lowers the no-drop LRW score from 84.60% to 82.40%, but at five randomly dropped frames it raises accuracy from 32.94% to 68.74% (the authors state a 35.80-point gain). The variable-length TCN scores 85.30% with no frames removed and 71.49% with five removed, avoiding the BGRU full-sequence tradeoff in these reported conditions.

questions.q: How should the reported generalization and noise robustness be bounded?
questions.answer: The paper tests random frame deletion on LRW and babble-noise conditions, not a documented cross-speaker, cross-session, or external-corpus evaluation. The split identities, overlap controls, seeds, validation/checkpoint selection, input normalization, chance baseline, and details of the babble-noise test set are not reported.

questions.q: Was the final reported training recipe strictly trained from scratch?
questions.answer: The authors say scratch training is feasible, but also state that they adopt pretraining on the hardest 10% of LRW words (50 classes) because it speeds training and slightly improves performance. The selection list is attributed to [10], without further selection-data details.

questions.q: Reader question Q1 (comparators: temporal back ends, staged training, best prior and current LRW / LRW-1000 results)
questions.answer: Yes. On LRW's evaluation/test split, N2 (temporal-convolution back end) reports 74.6% top-1; the best Bi-LSTM configuration, N7, reports 83.0%. Word boundaries are not used. Training is staged: temporal convolution first, then Bi-LSTM training with the front end fixed, then end-to-end training.

questions.q: Reader question Q2 (comparators: temporal back ends, staged training, best prior and current LRW / LRW-1000 results)
questions.answer: For the comparable no-boundary Table 11 configurations, V4 TConv has 22.51% MCR and V6 BiLSTM has 17.01% MCR. The best BiLSTM result is V15 at 11.92% MCR, using word-boundary indicators. No random temporal augmentation is described; the paper does describe boundary-based out-of-word frame removal that produces variable-length sequences.

questions.q: Reader question Q3 (comparators: temporal back ends, staged training, best prior and current LRW / LRW-1000 results)
questions.answer: The best LRW test top-1 accuracy is 84.07%. The model uses a two-stream I3D/deep 3D CNN front end with ImageNet-initialized weights followed by Kinetics pretraining, and a Bi-LSTM back end.

questions.q: Reader question Q4 (comparators: temporal back ends, staged training, best prior and current LRW / LRW-1000 results)
questions.answer: Table 1's matched scratch recipe (Crop, Flip, Mixup and Time Masking on; boundary indicators on) gives DC-TCN 92.1%, MS-TCN 90.0% and BGRU 89.7%, all without external pretraining. The best self-distilled single model/ensemble scores are 93.5%/94.1% with LRS2&3+AVS pretraining; without external data, the abstract reports 92.8%/93.4%.

questions.q: Reader question Q5 (comparators: temporal back ends, staged training, best prior and current LRW / LRW-1000 results)
questions.answer: The accuracy columns are LRW without word-boundary indicators, LRW(WB), and CAS-VSR-W1K (LRW-1000), respectively: 93.2 ± 0.1, 95.0 ± 0.0, and 58.2 ± 0.0. Yes, these are averaged across three experiments; ± denotes standard deviation.
